title: Diurnal effects of dynamic lighting on alertness, cognition, and mood of mentally fatigued individuals in a daylight deprived environment
research_question: This study investigated the non-image forming (NIF) effects of dynamic light on alertness, cognitive performance and mood on mental fatigue, as well as moderation of task difficulty in lighting perception.

participants.description: 16 college students (8 males, 8 females) aged 22–26 years (mean age=24) with science and engineering majors (excluding lighting), no eye complaints/color vision deficiencies, no drinking/smoking, no jet lag/night shift in the month prior, non-extreme chronotypes (MEQ), no sleep problems (PSQI≤7). Participants maintained regular work and rest cycles (wake-up 07:00-09:00, bed 22:00-00:00).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies recruitment from a university setting based on description.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Confined lit room (3m x 2m x 2.8m) with white cloth walls. Two lighting conditions: Static Lighting (SL) at 4000K CCT and Dynamic Lighting (DL) with CCT ranging from 4000K to 12000K in a linear function form. Illuminance was kept constant at approximately 500 lx on the desk for both. DL involved 16-step changes (500K increments) from 4000K to 12000K and back, with a 50-minute cycle (94 seconds per step, 47 seconds for 4000K/12000K initiation/termination). All lighting had CRI ≥ 80 and no perceived flickering. Melanopic EDI ranged from 224 lx (4000K) to 420 lx (12000K).

measures.instrument: Brunel Mood Scale (BRUMS) - 6 subscales (Anger, Confusion, Depression, Fatigue, Tension, Vigour), 4 items each, 5-point Likert (0-4)
Positive Affect and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) - 10 positive, 10 negative adjectives, 5-point Likert (1-5)
Multi-Attribute Task Battery-II (MATB-II) - System Monitoring, Tracking, Resource Management (low, medium, high difficulty)
National Aeronautics Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) - 6 dimensions
Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) - P300 amplitude and latency at Fz, Cz, Pz, Oz electrodes
Saliva samples, enzyme linked immunosorbent assay

findings.mechanism: Increased task demands lead to higher perceived difficulty.
findings.quote: significant differences in subjective ratings under different task difficulties (F2,15=78.77, p<0.001, R2=0.91)

findings.mechanism: Increased task demands lead to higher perceived workload.
findings.quote: Differences in overall scores of NASA-TLX under different task difficulties were statistically significant (F2,78=71.77, p<0.001, R2=0.72)

findings.mechanism: Higher task difficulty consumes more cognitive resources, leading to poorer performance.
findings.quote: comprehensive scores were significantly influenced by the task difficulty (F2,73=5.04, p<0.05, R2=0.59), with performance decreased significantly with the increase of the task difficulty

findings.mechanism: Static, lower CCT lighting may not adequately support alertness, leading to increased sleepiness after cognitive load.
findings.quote: KSS scores under SL were significantly higher than those under BL (p<0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic light exposure helped maintain vigilance at baseline levels, preventing an increase in sleepiness.
findings.quote: KSS scores did not significantly differ between DL and BL (p>0.05), indicating that dynamic light exposure could maintain vigilance at the same level as baseline.

findings.mechanism: Static lighting may not support positive emotional states, especially after mental fatigue.
findings.quote: positive mood under the SL was significantly lower than that under the BL (p<0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting helps maintain positive mood, preventing decline after mental workload.
findings.quote: no significant changes were observed after the DL exposure (p>0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting provides a more comfortable atmosphere perception, improving positive mood compared to static lighting.
findings.quote: positive mood was significantly lower under SL than under DL (p<0.001)

findings.mechanism: Static lighting may exacerbate negative emotional states after mental fatigue.
findings.quote: negative mood increased significantly after the SL exposure (p<0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting helps inhibit negative mood after long-term mental workload tasks.
findings.quote: no significant difference was found between the DL and BL (p>0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting helps inhibit negative mood compared to static lighting.
findings.quote: negative mood was significantly higher under SL versus DL (p<0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic light, possibly due to higher CCT exposure or light dynamics, acutely enhances sustained attention.
findings.quote: The participants had faster reaction speed under DL than under SL.

findings.antecedent: Lighting condition (SL vs DL) x Task difficulty (n-back: 0-back, 1-back, 2-back)

findings.quote: interaction between lighting conditions and task difficulty was significant for the RT (F2,56=4.00, p<0.05, R2=0.81)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting improves working memory performance even at low cognitive load.
findings.quote: RT was longer under SL than DL among 0-back (p<0.05)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting improves working memory performance at moderate cognitive load.
findings.quote: RT was longer under SL than DL among... 1-back (p<0.01)

findings.quote: RT was longer under SL than DL among... 2-back (p<0.01)

findings.mechanism: Increased task demands lead to lower accuracy.
findings.quote: Only the significant main effect of task difficulty on ACC was found (F2,86=6.71, p<0.05, R2=0.13).

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting enhances executive control function, leading to better overall task performance.
findings.quote: main effect of lighting condition on comprehensive scores was significant (F1,72=6.83, p<0.05, R2=0.62), suggesting that participants performed better under DL than under SL regardless of task difficulty.

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting reduces the subjective effort required for tasks.
findings.quote: main effect of lighting condition was found in the two indexes of ‘physical demand' (F1,77=8.30, p<0.05, R2=0.57)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting reduces negative emotional responses to task demands.
findings.quote: and 'frustration' (F1,77=8.94, p<0.05, R2=0.76). The results of a post-hoc test showed that the participants felt lower physical demand and frustration under DL versus SL (all p<0.05).

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting increases the allocation of attentional resources and arousal, reflected by larger P300 amplitudes.
findings.quote: main effect of lighting condition was significant for the P300 amplitudes at Cz (F1,57=4.12, p<0.05, R2=0.10)

findings.mechanism: Dynamic lighting increases the allocation of attentional resources and arousal, reflected by larger P300 amplitudes.
findings.quote: Oz (F1,57=4.88, p<0.05, R2=0.59). There was no significant main effect of the task difficulty or significant lighting condition× task difficulty interaction on P300 amplitude. Post-hoc comparisons showed that the amplitude was larger under DL than under SL conditions.

findings.antecedent: Lighting condition (SL vs DL) x Testing period (before vs after exposure)
findings.mechanism: Daytime light exposure, even dynamic, may not significantly suppress melatonin, which is typically at its lowest during the day.
findings.quote: no significant difference in the salivary melatonin levels between SL and DL conditions (F1,48=2.53, p>0.05, R2=0.11)

mechanisms: Dynamic light, potentially due to higher CCT or the dynamic changes themselves, activates retinal photoreceptors (ipRGCs) to support arousal levels.
Light information is transmitted to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) or amygdala, and further to brain regions (e.g., locus coeruleus) related to alertness and cognition.
Dynamic lighting increases the input of attentional resources in cognitive processing of the brain, as indicated by larger P300 amplitudes.
Dynamic lighting reduces subjective workload (physical demand, frustration) associated with tasks.
Dynamic lighting provides a more comfortable atmosphere perception, which helps maintain positive mood and inhibit negative mood.
implementation_implications: Dynamic lighting could be applied to improve alertness, cognitive performance, and positive mood of fatigued individuals in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments with daylight deprivation.
Appropriate dynamic lighting manipulation can provide comfortable atmosphere perception and help meet demands for stress recovery in engineering applications.

tables.description: Photometric parameters at eye level for the typical lighting conditions (4000K, 6000K, 8000K, 12000K CCTs), including illuminance, CCT, total irradiance, CRI, and spectrally weighted a-opic irradiances (melanopsin, S-cone, M-cone, L-cone, Rods).
Statistics of PSQI and MEQ scores for the test participants (Min, Max, Mean, Standard deviation).
The MATB-II with three difficulty levels, specifying events/minute for SYSMON, update/response for TRACK, and pump failures/minute for RESMAN, along with duration.

Results of the LMM analyses for VAS and BRUMS scores across baseline, first fatigue induction, and second fatigue induction, including EMM ± SD, F-statistic, df, p-value, R², and post-hoc comparisons.

Results of the LMM analyses for subjective measures (KSS, PANAS Positive, PANAS Negative) under Baseline, Static Lighting, and Dynamic Lighting conditions, including EMM ± SD, F-statistic, df, p-value, and R².

limitations: Compliance with the imposed sleep-wake schedule for the nights before the experimental session was not monitored (e.g., using actigraphy or sleep diaries).

The study provides preliminary support for DL advantages in countering mental fatigue, but practical applications are complex and multidimensional; future studies should manipulate multi-dimensional fatigue levels.
Sex differences were not tested due to the study focus and small sample size.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Diurnal effects of dynamic lighting on alertness, cognition, and mood of mentally fatigued individuals in a daylight deprived environment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This study investigated the non-image forming (NIF) effects of dynamic light on alertness, cognitive performance and mood on mental fatigue, as well as moderation of task difficulty in lighting perception. Sixteen participants completed a psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) and two complex cognitive tasks (multi-attribute task battery-II (MATB-II) and n-back) with low, medium and high difficulty levels under dynamic (4000 to 12 000 K, melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) = 224 lx to 420 lx) and static (4000 K, melanopic EDI = 224 lx) lighting with illuminance set at 500 lx on the desk. Psychological, behavioural, biochemical and electrophysiological responses to light were assessed. The results showed that exposure to dynamic light had significant benefits on subjective sleepiness, positive mood and task performance, which may be moderated by task difficulty. The intervention effect of dynamic light on fatigue was also found during an electrophysiological activity due to increase in the amount of attentional resources allocated to the tasks by dynamic light, but was not observed in biochemical measures.
